utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. For the sake of the record, could we have the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Judge Clark, Your Honour, Judge Diarra. Kenneth Scott for the Office of the Prosecutor together with Mr. Poriouvaev, Mr. Bos, and Ms. Fleming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. Kresimir Krsnik and I'm accompanied by Christopher Meek as co-counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Naletilic, can you hear the proceedings in a language you understand? THE ACCUSED NALETILIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We haven't seen each other for almost five months. How are you feeling? I mean, how about your health? THE ACCUSED NALETILIC: [Interpretation] Thank you for asking. It's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have anything to complain during that period? THE ACCUSED NALETILIC: [Interpretation] No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. This is a special hearing based on the schedule order rendered by this Trial Chamber on the 18th March 2003. This Trial Chamber received the motion for stay of further deliberation of the evidence on an expedited request for the taking of further evidence in light of newly disclosed material provided by the OTP filed by Defence counsel of Mr. Naletilic on March 12th, 2003. In this motion, the Defence believes that this material would have been helpful, if not essential, to the Defence. And had it been available during the trial, it would have impacted on the preparation of the case, as well as in cross-examination of certain witness. On March 14th, 2003 this Trial Chamber got the Prosecutor's response, in which the Prosecutor claimed the document was reviewed and found not fall within Rule 68. The Prosecution nevertheless decided to provide the document to the Defence out of abundant caution and good faith. Yesterday we received the Prosecutor's further response, stating that part of the document was disclosed to Defence on May 28th, 2002 as a Prosecution Exhibit P424.1 and used in the testimony of Defence Witness NW on September 3rd, 2002 and used again with Prosecution Witness Idrizovic. As a general rule, evidence other than exculpatory material may not be tendered after the final closure of the trial proceedings in court. Rule 68 establishes a continuing obligation on the Prosecution to disclose to the Defence without any specific time limit but as soon as practicable the existence of any exculpatory material known to the Prosecution. The purpose of this hearing is to ascertain the positions of the parties as to the possible exculpatory nature of the document, including for the Prosecution to clarify its reason for submitting the document if it did not think it was exculpatory, and for the Defence to establish prima facie that the document fall under Rule 68 of the Rules by showing just where and how it contains exculpatory information. Since the Defence counsel filed this motion, we would like to hear Mr. Krsnik on this matter first. Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as you have started, with respect to disclosure of evidence of an exculpatory nature, I must admit that perhaps my English was not quite correct because we wrote this motion very rapidly, because on the 5th of March I received these documents in my office in the Croatian language, and unfortunately there is no translation at the moment. I think we're all handicapped because of this. I will try to read out the main parts of some of the documents slowly so that you too, Your Honours, might gain insight into the character of these documents. And these documents shed new light on the events in Sovici and Doljani, these events that we have discussed at length over a two-year period here. First of all, Your Honours, I would like to say that this collection of records from the Mijat Tomic Battalion was positioned in Sovici and Doljani. And so that these could be visually portrayed to you, it has to do with a book in which minutes were taken from the 9th of February, 1993 up until the 25th of July, 1993. What concerns Defence counsel is the fact that certain dates are missing. If someone has this notebook, then that person has all the minutes too. And what the Prosecutor refers to when he said that one of these documents from this collection was disclosed to us, that is correct, but that also shows that he had all the other documents at the time because they're all contained in one notebook. We found this document here too, but Mr. Meek will address this issue. Our position, Your Honours, is that these documents exist -- all of the documents exist, and our learned colleagues from the Prosecution have had them since 1996. Otherwise, they wouldn't have been in a position to have these -- this document that they gave to Witness NV [As interpreted], as they said in their response to your submission. These documents confirm everything that the Defence counsel has been saying for two years. These are documents that are in accordance with the indictment that was issued in the court in Konjic and we had great difficulty in getting them -- obtaining them from the Prosecution and we didn't obtain all of them. These documents point to what we have been claiming was the case all the time, all along. They show that part of the 4th Corps of the BH army was in Sovici, they were armed, they dug trenches. But I'm going to read out certain parts to you. Who took the civilians, the captured civilians away? Who fed them? It's all stated here. But naturally, my client doesn't appear anywhere. Likewise -- he doesn't appear anywhere in the indictment in Konjic -- likewise the indictment in Konjic doesn't appear anywhere. What is also interesting is hat it is not at all in accordance with parts of the famous, of the notorious Alojz Rados diary. And it would appear, at least according to the signature here, that he took these minutes of the meetings and according to the signature it seems that the same man took these minutes, that is to say, Alojz Rados. We're a little tired now. I think we're all here for the sake of justice and especially the Prosecution is here for the sake of justice. This isn't an institution that persecutes. It's an institution that wants to render justice. They're in a different position than that of the Defence. And it is not our intention to attack the Prosecution. This wouldn't even cross my mind. I've already expressed my position with regard to the Prosecution before this Trial Chamber, and I'm not going to repeat what my position is. I think it's quite clear. I have often repeated that the Prosecution in this Tribunal isn't acting in good faith and this is proved from day to day. But as I said, my intention is not to attack them, but we would like to hear why these minutes weren't disclosed to the Defence during the proceedings. On several occasions Defence counsel asked the Prosecution to provide them with material that related to the indictment and especially to Sovici and Doljani. This is what we did throughout the proceedings, as you are well aware, Your Honours. And I cannot agree with the claim of my learned colleagues according to which these minutes that I have just received now, these minutes from the meetings of the Mijat Tomic Battalion correspond in full to other documents, conform fully to other documents which Rados, a certain Rados prepared, as the Prosecution says. And this also shows that these minutes aren't consistent according to the thesis of the Prosecution and this is why we wanted to inform this Trial Chamber of these matters, for the sake of justice. The Prosecution accepts these documents. They say that there was someone called Rados. The Prosecution relies on these documents. The Defence does not have to do that. But this contradicts the Prosecution's basic and main thesis that there were unarmed civilians in Sovici, that the attack was imagined, the attack to expel Muslims, et cetera, et cetera. And these are documents quite clearly states what is the case, what happened throughout the relevant period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think the President asked you to be more concise in your address to us in that you have to tell us specifically what in these documents is exculpatory material and not confirmatory of a state of affairs which existed in Sovici and Doljani before the 16th or 17th of April. Can you address yourself very specifically to what information is in those documents which would -- very good. Well, if you'd come to that instead of the other things that you've been addressing us in relation to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for your comment. You know, there are a lot of documents, and I had to make a few introductory comments, but I hope that we are all familiar with the subject matter now. But as you can see, there are a lot of documents that I have prepared and I also wanted to respond to the Prosecutor's last motion, and I didn't have the opportunity to do so before. You know, we received these documents at the eleventh hour as they say in my country, and I don't think this is really fair. And the Prosecution does admit that they had them in January, although we can also see that the Prosecution had these documents in 1996. Your Honour, I had to write this in my -- using my knowledge of English and submit it immediately, not just to inform you but perhaps because of appeals. And there are 153 Pages here. And I'll be more specific, now, why are these documents more important? I've got it all written down and I'll read it out to you. The documents are important because contrary to what the Prosecution claims and the witness who claimed with regard to Sovici and Doljani that the BH army was in Sovici, who claimed that in Sovici and around Sovici the BH army dug trenches before April. On the 9th of February, 1993 they used heavy machines to dig trenches. And on the 10th of February, 1993 there was a meeting of the BH HVO -- of the BH army and the HVO in Jablanica and this meeting was attended by Zajko Sahiljic, Dzemal Ovnovic, and Dino Senad they represented the BH army, and Marko Zelenika, Stipo Pole, and Alojz Rados were present and they discussed the relation and the conflict between the people and the units of the BH army and the HVO in the area of Doljani and Sovici. Your Honour, there is a lot of material here. I don't want to skip things. I wanted to inform you of everything. This is the order in which I have marked everything that I can read out, because unfortunately you don't have these documents in English, so you are handicapped. If you'd been able to familiarise yourself with them before, then I would be able to discuss this matter in a different manner. But now you have to wait to see what I'm going to inform you of because you haven't had the opportunity of reading these documents. So Dzemal Ovnovic admits with regard to these trenches, he admits that hey belonged to the 4th Corps of the BH army. This appears in this document. That contradicts the claim that the people were unarmed. It says that the BH army had a checkpoint in Sovici on the 25th of March, 1993. And then there is an entire list of other things. I'll try to be brief and refer to concrete events. And this shows, without a doubt, Your Honours, that in Sovici and Doljani there were armed forces that were involved in a conflict. It wasn't a matter of the civilian population. And this was a conflict between the HVO and the BH army. If we had had this when the Prosecution witnesses appeared - and I'm not going to repeat what their testimony was with regard to Sovici and Doljani - if we had been able to ask questions about this and if we had been aware of contents of these documents, I think that our cross-examination would have been quite different. And now, as far as the documents are concerned which appear after the 16th of April, these documents quite clearly mention the fact that the Mijat Tomic Battalion took care of supplying and feeding the people and prisoners. Likewise, that civilians were placed in Junuzovici, were accommodated in Junuzovici, that they looked after cattle, et cetera, how they're going to accommodate civilians who are captured, how they're going to treat them, et cetera, these decisions are decisions that were taken and implemented by the Mijat Tomic Battalion and not -- this was not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. something done by Mr. Naletilic, as the indictment states. A series of documents also talks about how food for civilians, captured civilians, was organised, about how supplies were provided, not just of food but also medical provisions, toiletries, et cetera. They mention how cattle -- how livestock was looked after, who looked after livestock. They emphasise the problems of looting property, et cetera, and they apologise about this. And what is most important, it talks about how the departure of civilians from Sovici and Doljani was organised, who organised it, who escorted them, et cetera. And my client doesn't appear in this respect at any point. And now, the Prosecution says that our arguments aren't justified. We can't inform you of all the important details apart from the ones that I have mentioned. I'm just going to try and read out two or three of these details. But in the opinion of the Defence counsel, the fact, Your Honours, that in Sovici and Doljani parts of the 4th Corps of the BH army were present - so it wasn't a matter of civilian population - we consider this fact to be of such importance that we would have used it in the course of our cross-examination without a doubt. The Defence counsel hasn't changed its opinion about Rados's diary. The Defence counsel claimed that this diary was modified in order to justify a thesis, and this is what was shown. What happened to the diary? What happened with the diary? You witnessed this as I did. The Defence counsel received a typed version, and afterwards we received a photocopy of the alleged original. And when the Prosecution's last witness appeared, we received the original diary for inspection. That was nothing new. Likewise, the Defence counsel can't claim that this material is authentic. We cannot claim this, and we can't deny it either. We simply have to investigate the matter. But the information contained in this document point to the fact that they contradict the claims made by the witnesses presented by the Prosecution. Similarly we think that the Prosecution is wrong when the subsequently provided material -- when they compare the subsequently provided material to the diary. We had the possibility of examining, investigating the diary, whereas this document, we've only had a cursory glance at it. We read through it very rapidly. We had to do this rapidly in order to carry out all -- take all the relevant steps in order to inform the Trial Chamber. We claimed certain things for a year and a half and this document was somewhere on the Prosecution's shelves throughout this period, and we were provided with the document at the eleventh hour, as I said. And finally, I would just like to say that Mladen Naletilic has the right for the Trial Chamber to be informed about all the events and circumstances for which -- or with which he's being charged and he has the right of being provided with these documents in the course of the proceedings that have been instituted against him. And these documents have been in the hands of the Prosecution since 1996. The indictment was issued in 1998. So is it possible to argue that the Prosecution has so many documents, is it possible to make such an argument before this International Tribunal and that for this reason we are not in a position to be provided with this document? Is that an argument, to say that we have too many documents, we've been inundated with documents and these are documents that the Defence was not able to use? I'll just read out a few items which I consider to be the most important ones. For example, at a meeting held on the 30th of March, 1993 all the commanders were present, all the commanders of the battalion were present, and it says that the entire territory of Jablanica was blocked, that there were additional checkpoints which were used, and then they mention the checkpoints that were set up by the BH army and Doljani and Sovici were surrounded, then they discuss the measures that should be taken in order to come to an agreement with the BH army and then the suggestion was made that discussions should be held with the BH army, with the Muslims, and they said that they should try to get rid of the checkpoints, and especially the checkpoint in Sovici. You know that all the witnesses, the Prosecution also claimed that there were never any -- there was never any such checkpoint. Furthermore, it states that this has to be presented in the command of the army and of the command of the HVO and similarly these documents quite clearly state who the commander is and what the high command post of Sovici and Doljani is. It quite clearly states here that it's in the Tomislavgrad area and that the commander is Mr. Siljeg, he should be informed of everything. This all contradicts the claims of the Prosecution according to which it is my client who is concerned. My client does not appear in these documents. Everything is stated here quite clearly. On the 10th of April, six days before the conflict broke out, singularly there was a meeting which was held and these are the problems that they emphasise, if there is a conflict, if a conflict breaks out. The military targets which the Mijat Tomic Battalion should deal with is combat the activity of the Muslims in Sovici and Doljani, to prevent the joining up of the forces from Jablanica with Doljani and Sovici. Three, to protect our features in Sovici and Doljani. And this contradicts the claim that someone came on the 16th of April in order to attack unarmed civilians and to expel them. There is a chronological order -- I won't bother you any more. I'll give the Prosecution the opportunity to have addressing you. But I just want to read out these most important things. "On the 21st of April, there was a meeting after the conflict --" that is to say, it mentions organising food for prisoners in Sovici, the transportation of food. And then there's another interesting thing, that's the terrain. It's in Sovici, contrary to what the Prosecution said according to which the Convicts Battalion was involved. Here it quite clearly says who was involved in mopping up the terrain, combing the terrain. So on that meeting in April the tasks are to comb the terrain, continue with combing the terrain. All those who are dead and wounded should be recorded, the dead should be buried, et cetera, et cetera. It's very clear who was involved in mopping up and combing the terrain. I think this information is very important and it contradicts what the Prosecution has been claiming to date. Minutes taken on the 6th of May, 1993, Your Honours: "The other captured civilians shall be transferred to a certain location. This shall be done and coordinated by Ivan Rajic, it does not say Mladen Naletilic. It says Ivan Rajic. Transport shall be provided with military vehicles, lorries with tarpaulins, and escort will be provided by the command of the military police and that is what the command of the military police testified about before you. But the Prosecution -- what does the Prosecution say? They say that the Convicts Battalion did that, and some witnesses testified about this. Furthermore, the military police is also given the task of preventing looting, stealing, et cetera. About this document which is of particular interest, you will hear from my colleague, Mr. Meek. This is the document that I was given by the Prosecution when the Prosecution witness NW was on the stand. Your Honours, I tried to be very brief and concise and specific, pointing out only to certain things. Of course all events up to the 10th of April are covered, just as -- just for instance, there is a meeting of the 10th of February. All this needs to be translated. Dzemal Ovnovic head of the BH army said this -- do you think I had this when he was on the stand? He says: "The trenches that are being dug, let them be dug." He is now talking about Sovici. It is noted that machinery is being used in digging trenches in Sovici. I am looking for this place because I want to be as specific as possible. He notes and explains what trenches these are. He says, "The problem of trenches would be resolved if your people would be -- could be in Borovnik because nobody has anything against you from Donji Mahala but I don't believe people from outside. I don't trust people from outside," says Stipo Pole commander from the HVO. "I agree. But how can we explain this to our people if even in the army units we have representatives from outside." He means members from outside who are not from Sovici and Doljani. "How can we explain this if these outsiders even man the checkpoint?" Then follows a discussion. They discussed all these problems at many meetings, clearly stating their position in military terms. And Marko Zelenika says, "All these problems have been presented by us to the higher command, namely Commander Siljeg." I don't want to take any more of your time, Your Honour. I just singled out some examples in the brief time I have at my disposal, and I believe these examples corroborate the argument of the Defence that this material is not only contrary to the case of the Prosecution and the claims of its witnesses but also that if the Defence had had this document in time, we would have conducted our cross-examination completely differently. This type of document should not be handed to us at the eleventh hour. My colleague, Mr. Meek, will continue. Thank you for your understanding and thank you for holding this hearing today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, greetings from Kansas. It's good to be back in The Hague. I won't take very much of your time, not as much, I don't believe, as I probably should. I noticed, Your Honours, and I just had a chance to look at this and I'm a little hampered because this is all in Serbo-Croatian, and I'm relying on the discussions I've had with Mr. Krsnik and Ms. Pinter in regards to what this document actually says, and I believe Mr. Krsnik succinctly gave you several examples of how these documents, this 153-page document, allegedly authored by Rados, contradicts the Prosecution theory in this case in regards to Sovici and Doljani. Exculpatory evidence, Your Honours, as I understand it - and I don't have the definition in front of me - is any evidence which would tend to demonstrate the innocence of the accused or would tend to mitigate punishment of the accused. If you look at the indictment against Mr. Naletilic, you see that the Prosecution has charged him in three areas, basically, Sovici-Doljani in April, Mostar, and also Rastane. Certainly, Your Honours, I don't see how the Prosecution can argue that if Mr. Naletilic could have been shown to have no active role or even a role as active as alleged by the Prosecution in Sovici and Doljani and could be cut out of that conflict that that in itself would not have been -- would not mitigate his punishment if he were convicted in this case. So to say that this evidence, these documents, which as I've said before and I may repeat again - I don't understand them. I don't read this language. They have not been translated into English. Apparently there have been 33 excerpts that the Prosecution has deemed relevant enough to translate in English with the hopes of use of cross-examination of Defence witnesses but they did not use but one, 424.1, I think. In looking at these documents, Your Honour, I see that in the original -- a copy of the original 152 pages the two pages which were translated and became Prosecution Exhibit 424.1 have this bate stamp of 02181733 and 734. However, if you look at the Bates stamp on the same two items, which would have been the minutes of the meeting of 30th of May 1993, they are Bates stamp numbers of 01174655 and 56. The Bates stamp numbers don't match, which indicates to me, and I'm sure that Mr. Scott can enlighten this Trial Chamber and enlighten Defence counsel why that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. might be, but it would appear that there were obviously two copies, at least two copies in the Office of the Prosecutor of this 153-page document, otherwise it would be a factual impossibility to have different Bates numbers on these two pages to 30 May 1993 minutes from the meeting as I've set forth. In the filing of the Prosecutor yesterday 19 March 2003 attached is the B/C/S version handwritten of the two pages, again last three numbers 733, 734. Those will match identically with 655, and 656 in the 153-page document that has been sent to Defence counsel very recently. Frankly, Your Honours, I find this to be disheartening and I am concerned about several issues. The Prosecutor frankly and fairly admits in paragraph 2 that they did in fact receive the 153-page compilation of the Mijat Tomic Brigade minutes. When did they receive it? Mr. Krsnik alleges approximately 1996, when this case began to be investigated. Perhaps Mr. Scott or someone from the Prosecution can enlighten us how long they have had these documents. Paragraph 3 of their motion yesterday, the further response, they talk about April 2002, approximately one year ago, that a hard copy of these minutes were reviewed by some members of the Prosecution investigation team. And then they go on to state that four parts were selected for possible cross-examination. Which members of the Prosecution/investigation team reviewed this 153-page document back in April of 2002, decided to have four excerpts translated into English to present to Defence witnesses on cross-examination? We would like to know who they were. Eventually under paragraph 5 they indicate that only two pages P424.1 were actually disclosed to the Defence. Again, made -- a call made by the Prosecution. But to revert back to paragraph 4 of their motion yesterday, the Prosecution states, "Those who reviewed the document at the time --" again, we'd like to know who it was that reviewed the documents. These are very, very capable qualified attorneys representing the Prosecution in this case. They also state in paragraph 4 that they determined this material was not covered by Rule 68, that it was not exculpatory, and therefore they did not have a duty to give it to us. Your Honours, this has been a continuing problem in this Trial Chamber and I think in this Tribunal, and that is simply that the Prosecution gets to choose and gets to make a determination on what evidence they believe to be exculpatory. We made some requests - I don't recall when; the record will reflect - that we be allowed to look at all documents even if we have to look at them in Prosecutor's office to determine if we believed that they were exculpatory to our client for our theory of the defence. And I believe that the only proper rule in this Tribunal should be that only the Defence counsel can make a decision on what evidence is exculpatory to their theory of the defence, to their theory of the accused. This is an adversary proceeding. As we all know in an adversarial proceeding we can't rely on our adversary to look after our best interest. And this appears to be a situation that the Prosecutor had determined at some point they didn't believe this to be exculpatory until a week before the judgments to be rendered and then they decided whoops, we forgot this document, it's 153 pages, apparently written by the same person that we claim wrote the Rados diary, a man by the name of Alojz Rados, which was hard -- a very hard-fought battle, if you will recall, about that whole diary, whether that was admissible, what the relevance was, was it authentic. We fought tooth and nail about that, Your Honours, and I don't even have to remind you of that. And that's what the Prosecutor says in his further motion, that they just believed that in an abundance of caution and in good faith they would supply us these, even though they didn't believe they needed to. Well, Your Honours, again, I am hampered, as you are. I wish this was in English so I could read this entire thing, this entire 153 pages, and have a right to consult with my client along with my leading counsel, Mr. Krsnik, in a setting that we all know what is being said in this diary or in this 153 pages written by the same person that was supposed to have written the diary that's been admitted over strenuous objection. How good of faith can it be when the Prosecution knew how strenuous and continuously we objected to the admission of the Rados diary and they were sitting on 153 pages encompassing meetings of the HVO, Mijat Tomic Battalion in Sovici, which concerned a period of time predating the April 17th, April 18th conflict, into May, and past that time, where our client is not mentioned as a coordinator, as a commander, as being present prior to the 17th of April. If that doesn't contradict the evidence of the Prosecution, Your Honours, I frankly don't know what does. If that does not tend to demonstrate the innocence of Mr. Naletilic, or if you don't believe it goes that far, if that evidence doesn't tend to mitigate the damages or mitigate the possible punishment he might receive if he were cut out of Sovici, I don't know what does. This is exculpatory evidence under either prong of the fork. It either goes to show his innocence, which we submit it does, or it goes to mitigate his punishment, which we submit it would. In either fashion, this is exculpatory evidence. Again, we don't know how long the Prosecutors had it. We don't know which Prosecutors looked at it. We don't know which Prosecutors made the decision that this isn't exculpatory, we don't have to give it to the Defence. But that decision got reversed very recently. And Mr. Krsnik received this document on the 5th day of March. We filed a response as quickly as we could, on the 7th. What the only fair proper thing to do, Your Honours, is to stay the deliberation of the evidence in this case, have this document translated into English, allow us a reasonable time to investigate this matter, allow us the right to call the Prosecution witnesses who we believe we could have cross-examined differently and used this material in the cross-examination of those witnesses. In lieu of that, Your Honours, based on outrageous prosecutorial conduct in this matter by not disclosing this exculpatory evidence to us until a week before judgment, all claims in the indictment relating to Sovici, Doljani should be dismissed. We believe, Your Honour, that you may have more questions -- we can't question the Prosecutors, but I believe their further response filed yesterday raises many more questions than answers. I'm frankly shocked. I'm always shocked and amazed. But this is very relevant, highly relevant, highly exculpatory evidence that we would have put to good use had we had it in a timely fashion, which we did not. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we turn to the Prosecutor. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Your Honour, I'm not going to spend a great deal of the Court's time revisiting the facts that we've put before the Chamber in terms of the history of the document itself. I could sit here or stand here and give you exactly the same account that we've given to you in our filings. I hope the Chamber will see that throughout this entire history of events, including the initial disclosures, the sending of the document back in February, and the two responses that we have filed, including the second response to clarify what indeed we felt should be clarified, in every instance the Prosecutor's first instincts has been to be transparent and to disclose all that we could to assist the Chamber. Between the two filings that we have made, Mr. President, we have shown that -- and there is no dispute. There is no dispute -- that the document came into the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor in approximately March 1996. Through human error, which does happen occasionally, the document was not placed into the electronic database of the Office of the Prosecutor and therefore would not be produced as a result of -- in a response to subsequent electronic searches. Nonetheless, a hard copy of the document became known or was known to certain members of the Prosecution investigation team, and I must disagree with counsel that I don't see that there's anything to be gained by going into the names of those persons. We've told the Chamber quite clearly that our office, certain members of our office, did in fact -- were in fact aware of that document at an earlier time. It was reviewed. It was determined not to be Rule 68. There was no 66(B) disclosure request, as this Chamber knows, from the very early days of this trial, we spent a lot of time on those disputes about the documents and the discovery. There was no reason to turn the document over at that time. That was the assessment made by those who were familiar with the document at that time. And my subsequent assessment of the document in January and February agrees with that. It was the right decision then, and it was the right assessment now. Therefore, there was under the practice of the Tribunal no responsibility, no obligation whatsoever, for the Prosecutor to turn it over. It was not selected as a Prosecution exhibit. It was not subject to a Rule 66(B) request. It was not Rule 68. It was like thousands and thousands, millions of other documents possessed by the OTP; it was a document that was not selected for evidence in this case and was simply put aside. There were a few excerpts that were selected for potentially for use in cross-examination. Only one of them ultimately was used in court, as we've indicated, and that is Exhibit P424.1. What happened then is that subsequently, as we've said in our papers, the hard copy -- the hard copy of the document resurfaced, if you will, in January. It was brought to my attention and it was reviewed again, and again it was found not to be Rule 68 -- covered by Rule 68. Now, we've said repeatedly in the letter that I sent to Mr. Krsnik on the 17th of February and in our filings out of abundant caution, good faith, it was simply turned over. It was decided for the very reasons -- for the very reasons Mr. Meek just went on about, about the importance of the Rados diary -- we thought with the benefit of hindsight, since the Rados diary was indeed a hotly contested piece of evidence. That this document, though not in our view Rule 68 at all and in fact in our view fully consistent with the Prosecution case, in this particular circumstance it was, if you will, the better part of valour, the better part of discretion simply to make it available to them. And you will forgive me, Your Honour, if I -- what I'm about to say is -- I'm going to explain one thing in order to say what I'm going to say next. The Chamber may know that there is a biblical mandate about if one forces you to go 1 mile, go with them 2 miles, go to second mile. And when my -- if I can be, just give a personal explanation of this. When my wife asked me recently why the judgment had been postponed, I said, "Well, it appears that I'm in trouble for going the second mile," for turning over a document that we had no obligation to turn over but simply chose unbalanced that it was the easiest thing to do given the Rados diary and this document also prepared by Mr. Rados to simply turn it over to the Defence. The Defence has made -- I've listened carefully, and if the Chamber -- perhaps some of the Chamber and the Court staff have seen the movie Chicago, and there's a wonderful scene in the movie where the Defence lawyer does a tap dance scene. And I respectfully submit to the Chamber that's about all we've seen this afternoon. Neither Mr. Krsnik nor Mr. Meek, even after so directed by Her Honour Judge Clark, could ever give any specific answer to the question of how it was that this document is exculpatory, how it was that this document would have affected the cross-examination of a Prosecution witness in any way. Now, it is -- the burden is on the Defence in this situation, as the Chamber recognised in asking the Defence to speak first, to show this Chamber, to convince this Chamber that this document is exculpatory and that they have suffered some material prejudice from its nondisclosure. Before I continue on, I just want to repeat again, Mr. President, in our assessment it is not exculpatory and it is fully consistent with the Prosecution case. Let's just take -- assuming -- I say "assuming" that Mr. Krsnik has accurately characterised some of the entries that he's referred to, simply taking them at face value, how is any of that exculpatory? He talks about the fact that there were armed defenders in the vicinity of Sovici in mid-April 1993. Never contested, never in dispute. The evidence was that there were indeed Muslim men, armed, who put up a limited defence of the village when it was attacked on the 16th of April. There was indeed firing. There was indeed -- there were indeed weapons that -- remember, the weapons were confiscated by the HVO. They were turned in at one of the houses. Never a dispute, never a dispute that there were armed Muslim soldiers in the area. And in terms of something being exculpatory, it must relate to something in at issue in the case. The crimes concerning the attacks on Sovici -- the events in Sovici-Doljani do not charge unlawful attack. We go back to the basics, Mr. President: Look at the indictment. The indictment does not charge an unlawful attack on a civilian Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. population. What it does charge is forcible transfer after the attack, destruction of property after the attack, destruction of the mosque after the attack. Everything that Mr. Krsnik has said is simply irrelevant and not exculpatory in this slightest. I cite one additional example: Cikota was killed. He was killed in a hostile combat situation. That evidence alone shows that it was never in dispute that there was combat going on between two armed forces. The Defence really can't make up their mind whether they want to accept this document as true or -- or, if I can say, trash it along with the Rados diary. On the one hand they say it completely supports their case. On the one hand, they want to dismiss it out of hand. Even this afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, they have not made up their mind what their position is. These are the minutes of actual meetings of the local battalion leadership. They are different than the diary. These are not Mr. Rados's just broad observations. These are minutes of meetings, just simply meetings just as if any of us had been to board meetings, organisational meetings, PTA meetings, and minutes are taken. There's absolutely nothing exculpatory or particularly even interesting or noteworthy in the fact that if Mr. Naletilic wasn't present at a particular meeting of this local Battalion -- this was the local battalion -- that he wasn't involved in their regular meetings from February to July 1993 is not surprising at all, not -- and entirely not inconsistent for the Prosecution case. It's never been the Prosecution case - never- that he was the local kind of on-the-ground commander of the Mijat Tomic Brigade, never an issue, never asserted. The Bates stamp numbering, let me just address that that Mr. Meek raised. A complete answer: When the one -- when the document or the part which became Exhibit 424.1 was selected in approximately April 2002, it was at that time consistent with OTP practice given a Bates number and processed as a stand-alone document and a number was placed on it. When the document -- when the 153-page compilation was found in January, the entire document was processed again as a whole document and a new series of Bates numbers was given for the entire compilation. That's why the numbers are different. There have been various attacks on the diary. But lest there be any confusion, the diary is not in issue here, Mr. President. It's not what was in the diary that's at issue. It's these minutes. And whether these minutes standing and as the counsel have them and have asserted, whether these minutes are in any way exculpatory of the relevant issues in the case. And they have not told you that this afternoon and they cannot, because the Prosecution's assessment in April 2002 and in January 2003 was correct. They're not exculpatory. They're fully consistent with the Prosecution case. Even now, Mr. President, it's unfortunate that even now at this late date of these proceedings Mr. Krsnik says Mr. Tuta is not named in these documents and that makes it -- that in itself is exculpatory. Mr. President, if counsel is going to read parts of the document, he should make the Chamber aware of all parts of the document, including an entry on the 24th of April 1993 at 11.30 in the evening. "Finished. Commander Tuta arrived. Military activities start." Mr. President, there's been no showing. There's simply been no showing of anything exculpatory about this document or how it would have affected the Defence case in any way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm just going to be very brief. But, you know, I'm really at a disadvantage here, and I don't know how Mr. Scott unless he is now fluent in Serbo-Croatian, can understand this 153-page document, because I certainly can't read it. And how can he sit there and tell Your Honours that I don't know what I'm talking about? I told you I don't know what I'm talking about because they haven't translated this into English for me, so I have to go on what people tell me, just like he has to go on what people tell him. But it gets back to that basic assumption of why is it that the Prosecutor in this Tribunal gets to make the decision on what's exculpatory under Rule 66 and that is the law and that's set in concrete? That's what appears to be going on in this Trial Chamber and in other Trial Chambers. I'll let Mr. Krsnik take it from here, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't want to take much more of your time. The only thing I understood from the Prosecutor today was that I have to watch the academy award ceremony very carefully because there's a lot to learn from it, and I think everything is assuming film-making proportions and everything is going -- is proceeding as in a strange movie. Your Honours, the minutes from the meeting of the command staff of the battalion of the 6th of May, 1993, starting at 15.15 hours. Stipo Pole, Stipo Kopilas, Ivica Tomovic, Ivan Rajic, Jure Groznica, Ivo Zelenika and others attending. There are more names. The meeting chaired and led by Stipo Pole. Item 3 says "6th of May." That is precisely after -- I'm not going to repeat this, after the agreement between Petkovic and Halilovic about the change of population. Around this date the command of the battalion says, item 3, "The remaining captives, civilians --" I'm quoting from Croatian -- "the remaining captives, civilians, will be transferred to a designated place. This will be conducted and coordinated by Ivan Rajic. The transport shall be carried out by a freight vehicle, namely truck, with a tarpaulin," which means that it's a closed-covered truck, "whereas the escort shall be provided by a commander of the military police." It goes on to say: "Even in our army there are individuals and this is not allowed. That is why the military police will come." What follows is very illegible. I don't want to guess, but I think what it says is, "In order to prevent looting, robberies," this is not written in really learned language. The language is very simple. "Manipulations should not be allowed." And I'm asking you now, what are we claiming here -- what have we been claiming since 1998? What did the Prosecutor say? Who was responsible for the persecution and expelling of civilians? Who did that? And he is standing up here and saying -- he has the gall. Where does he get the gall to say that all this is not important? And he's been telling us all this time that my client is responsible for this. How can I qualify this sort of conduct when he now says that this document doesn't matter? It's just one example out of 153 pages. What was he saying about civilians? Who was persecuting them? Who was putting them in prison? Who put them in Junuzovici houses? What does the Prosecution say together with his witnesses, Mr. Naletilic is the Convicts Battalion. Look what the second document say, another document. Just one more document and I won't go reading any more because it's really not fair. It should have all been in English. "The meeting of the command held on the 21st of April, 1993, beginning at 1700 hours, the following persons attended: Stipo Pole, although it says Stipo S. Pole, Slaven, liaison officer for mortars, Zarinko Daric, A. Milicevic, Blaz Azinovic, Stipe Kopilas, Matan Zaric, Dr. V. Ljuban, Ivo Zelenika, and six more names. Not to waste any more time. Chaired by Stipo Pole." It says, "Accommodation of the troops, kitchen and food, secured through Posusje by Rogic. The pace of distribution of breakfast, dry-lunch," then says, "Hot --" with something illegible -- "and distribution of dry dinner and dry breakfast. Organisation of food for prisoners in Sovici, transport of food," and then it goes on to describe how all this is distributed. And this is just one example, Your Honours, about the organisation, distribution of food, the accommodation of prisoners. And just one more thing before I conclude. What has the Prosecutor, together with his witnesses, been claiming all the time? Who was in Sovici and who mopped up terrain, devastated, destroyed, burnt? The Convicts Battalion. And ipso facto Mr. Naletilic. Whereas here you read about a meeting - I singled this out - 24th April 1993 starting 11.00. Again, participants are listed, about a dozen names, submitting reports from the field. Here is one report: "Sovici. Most of the combing operation carried out and completed." So "combing and mopping up carried out. Continue with combing the terrain." One entry: "All dead and wounded should be recorded (Dr. Ljuban) and buried." And out of all names listed here, you will remember who testified here before you, Your Honours, we could have put some of these questions to them, couldn't we? We could have asked them about the authenticity about this document. Wouldn't that have held the justice and truth? What kind of explanation is this before an international court rendering international justice? Something like this couldn't happen in my village court in Croatia, believe me. That's all I have to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Questions by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I don't know whether we've been sitting too long and whether anybody needs a break, because any questions may cause both sides to address us further. Leaving aside for a moment, Mr. Krsnik and Mr. Meek, the misdemeanours or otherwise of the Prosecution and whether Mr. Scott is responsible under 7.1 or 7.3, it is your duty to assist us in relation to the allegations which you are making. Is there anything in that document which you have read which is exculpatory of your client in relation to the destruction of the mosque, the houses, the treatment of the prisoners of the fish farm, or the treatment and the guarding of the civilian prisoners in the Junuzovic -- I always have a problem -- Junuzovic houses and the school? Because as I understand you to say a few minutes ago, that there is something in those documents which indicates that the Mijat Tomic Brigade guarded the civilians in that hamlet. Now, that is capable of providing food for thought. But is there anything exculpatory in relation to the mosque, the burning of the houses, or the prisoners at the fish farm? That's what you have to address yourself to. Because, Mr. Krsnik, can I say one thing: What we don't want to happen or I would hope wouldn't happen is that an examination of these documents can introduce by the back door any strengthening of the Prosecution case, because that simply would not be fair. So be careful. Be careful if the document provides corroboration for anything or is capable of providing corroboration for anything which the Prosecution has alleged, because after all, when you think about it, the Mijat Tomic, when it has meetings in relation to its own business, is hardly likely to be dealing with the instructions which other commanders would give to their battalions. Do you understand me? I mean, there's nothing unusual about the commander of the Mijat Tomic Brigade dealing with the duties for their soldiers. It doesn't prove or disprove anything. It's neither probative nor exculpatory. So will you concentrate your mind on those issues, if you can, having read those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am very grateful. I have to say I've been reading these documents since the 5th of March every day. That's about 15 days now. That's what crossed my mind first of all. I didn't want the Prosecutor to laugh at me later on. I didn't want the Prosecutor to get something through the back door. I couldn't understand the reason for which the Prosecutor proceeded in this way, and that's why I examined this. And then, Your Honour, I understood how handicapped we had been and with impudence, if I may say so - and I hope I won't offend anyone by saying this - if I had had these documents, I would have examined the first five witnesses who claimed that they didn't have a single gun quite different. You know that they said that they didn't have any trenches at all. How do you think I would have examined those other witnesses, the witnesses who have been underlined here, my witnesses? That's the first matter. And then as far as exculpatory evidence is concerned, here the commander of the battalion issues an order as to what his subordinates should do, if I understand the Croatian language correctly. This should be viewed as a whole. And Your Honour, I am claiming that there are documents that are missing here. It's not complete. What we have been provided with is a selection, and I am claiming this categorically. Punish me if I am wrong. Why are there dates which are missing? Why does it say the 23rd of March and then it doesn't have the 28th and 29th but meetings were held every day and they're all contained in one notebook? And do you know why we're making this claim? Because of the document that we found. Do you see this one here? It has two different Prosecution numbers but they come from the same notebook. The Prosecutor gave them to me when we were examining the Witness NV [As interpreted] and he has also provided it now as part of this document. It's the same text but two -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. they have two different Prosecution numbers. How is this possible? I am claiming this is not complete. Not all the documents are contained here, and I fear that there may be other exculpatory documents from this book of documents and that's why they're not here. And Your Honour, as -- I'm not afraid that the Prosecution's thesis might be supported, and I am surprised by the fact that the Prosecutor managed to read this. It's confirmed here. On the 24th of April, the name of my client is mentioned. It says that he came -- I don't know whether it was Doljani or Sovici. And that's all. Is that forbidden? Or was that on the 16th? Doesn't that prove that he wasn't there when -- during the period for which you claim he was there? Your Honour, that's what I said. I am afraid that the Prosecution views the matters in this way. If I'd been in Sovici on the 16th, what would have happened then? Would I have ended up here as an accused also? So, Your Honour, I think that after all we have been through this can -- should all be translated and only then we will have a view of this, but I think that this entire notebook should be provided. You know, I'll never accept the claim that my client should be convicted because the Prosecution had too many documents or their database wasn't functioning. So should my client go to prison because the Prosecution was inundated with documents or because their database wasn't functioning? Are these proper arguments to be presented before an International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Leaving that aside, Mr. Krsnik, address me on this - it seems to be a good point that you're making and you made it a while ago - that there are documents that show that -- or you say that these documents indicate that the prisoners in the hamlet where the civilian women and children were taken was guarded by the Mijat Tomic and not by the Tutici or the Convicts Battalion. Address -- address us on that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking for the quote. Could you please grant me a minute or two or perhaps we could have a break. Mr. President, I don't know whether we need to have a break. [In English] I don't know really. I would like also to find all these sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think this hearing is approaching to its end. Shall we continue sitting here until it's finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course but just allow me to find the place, Your Honour, because I've marked all the relevant points here, all the relevant parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: It seemed to be the fifth point that you made, the fifth or the sixth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm looking for the quote. I want to find the exact quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You said -- after the 16th of April, Mijat Tomic took care of supplying and feeding persons. And then citizens were placed in Junuzovici houses and cared for them Mijat Tomic and not by Mr. Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's quite right, Your Honour. I'm trying to find the meeting where this occurred and where the subject was mentioned because I've mixed up the dates of the meetings. I'll find it in a minute, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in this case -- in this case, we might have a short break. We'll resume at 6.30. --- Break taken at 6.13 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I found two documents. Exactly talking about all of these questions Judge Clark was asking. [Interpretation] Perhaps I should be a little clearer. I am always afraid of the translation, et cetera. So I want to be clear. What are these documents? It's a collection, a collection of minutes of meetings. It has dates from the command of the Mijat Tomic Battalion. Each meeting is a separate document, has a separate document. Obviously it comes from one notebook. We don't have the original, but this is what I am assuming, a big notebook. And now, to answer Judge Clark's question: Immediately, we have two meetings that are specifically mentioned. The first was on the 20th of April, 1993 and it started at 10.00 hours. All the commanders and deputy commanders attended the meeting. I don't know if it's necessary for me to read out all their names, Stipo Pole, Stipe Kopilas, Milicevic, Ivo Zelenika, Ivica Tomic, Dr. Vlatko Ljuban, Darinko Azinovic, V. Antunovic, A. Rados, M. Krtic [phoen], and it says M. Zaric was also present, E. Rogic as well, and Jure Zelenika. Naturally these names are important for us. I should read them out so that we can remember who our witnesses were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, is that E. Rogic or I. Rogic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I., I. Rogic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Be careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, not E. -- I. I mean E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I for Ivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Ivan, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That's why I'm saying be careful. Remember what that witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes. But here, Your Honour, here is E. Rogic. [Interpretation] I don't want to translate the way the other side translated certain things. I want to read out what it says here. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And then this is what it says, "Sovici, another 14 soldiers from the BH army surrendered. Get organised for further action, for further action -- for further activities, and to take care of families. Doljani, the guards must be vigilant when performing their duties and they must find accommodation for population in houses." What else is important in this document dated the 20th of April? Well, it mentions other tasks. "Ivo Zelenika, with his men, should visit and search the area from Doljani to Ilijina Gruda, the entire area." That's what's contained on this document. And then on the 21st of April it continues and it mentions everything that you asked me about, Your Honour. The document isn't very long. Perhaps it wouldn't be a bad idea for me to read the entire document out to you. And it wouldn't take long to translate. It could be translated tomorrow it only consists of two pages because it's a separate document. This is what it states: "A meeting of the command held on the 21st of April, 1993 at 1700 hours. The following were present: S. Pole, Slaven, liaison, commander, mortar commander Darinko Azinovic, A. Milicevic, Blaz Azinovic, V. Antunov, it's probably Antunovic but it says "Antunov." You can't see the rest. Stijpe Kopilas, Matan Zaric - Zaric - Dr. V. Ljuban, Ivo Zelenika, Jure Groznica, Andjelko Rogic." And I can't read this. And then the next name is "Marko Rozic, Andrija Perkovic, and Jure Zelenika, Stipo Pole was the chairman: Accommodation provided for soldiers. Marko Rozic submitted the report," the canteen and food was secured via Posusje. A. Rogic. The distribution rhythm for breakfast, dry-lunch," and then I can't read what follows. And then it says, "Distribution of a dry-dinner ration too and also of a dry-breakfast, organising food for prisoners in Sovici the following item states transportation of food," and then the next item, "The commander Berkan, Juka, and Ivo each morning submit to the assistant to the commander the exact strength of troops." It says to the assistant commander. I don't know the name. I can see that there is a dot there, but the surname is Antunovic. "The strength of troops of our army should be worked out immediately. M. Rozic. The number of civilian prisoners, Ivica," the surname is illegible "and Blaz Azinovic by morning according to category. Women and children to be provided with accommodation in Memica Kuce, Memic's house, and security for Krkac. Provide food and they themselves should gather livestock and guard prisoners." So it says the tasks that they were given, "Supply food, guard livestock, and after that guard prisoners. All able-bodied men to the home in Doljani. Women and children to Junuzovici houses, the elderly to Sovici, and they are to look after the cattle, the livestock disarming. All arms -- all weapons are to be recorded via the logistics section according to their characteristics. There must not be any abuse. Such cases shall be severely punished. "Civilian authorities, include them in these activities to a greater extent. It's important to be aware of the numbers concerned, and they must be assembled." Then it says -- I'm not sure. I think it says, "Coordination -- coordinate to which positions are to be taken up. Medical care for the elderly, mostly for the elderly. A doctor shall be assigned." I think that the second page is missing because I can see that there is a list of items but I can't claim this for a fact because I don't know about this. But, Your Honour, from this record it's quite clear who adopted -- who issued the order, who distributed the tasks, ranging from taking care of civilians, feeding civilians, providing civilians with medical care, and guarding them. It's not a Supreme Command. It's not a high command. It's not according to orders from the high command. Here you quite clearly see who was in command and who assigns tasks. This document can be translated by tomorrow morning. It's a separate document. Read it. Similarly, the one dated the 30th of May, on the same meeting they assigned tasks according to which civilians should be taken to certain locations. And you know the kind of testimony we had here and you are aware of the witness who claimed the contrary and even mentioned my client. Here we can see that we have an individual order and we can see who issued the order, who distributed the task, and we can see who the people who were present are. And the date is the 21st of April. If this isn't exculpatory, I really don't know what is. Because if when the Prosecutor was writing the indictment, if he had this, he certainly wouldn't have said that my client -- that the Convicts Battalion was guarding the civilians, that they took them to prison, because that was claimed in the indictment and the Prosecution's witnesses claimed the same. But have a look at what it says here. It's not necessary to translate a lot of documents. We can translate two or three documents. Let's translate the document dated the 20th of April and the document dated the 6th of May, and I'll read it out to you once more. Again, there were ten people present, Stipo Pole, the commander, chaired the meeting and he assigned the following tasks: "The other civilian prisoners shall be transferred to designated locations." Again, it's a separate order. It states with the civilians are to go, and it states who is to guard them. It's the military police. We heard about this in testimony. It wasn't the Convicts Battalion who guarded them. When the unfortunate fate of Cikota was hence mentioned he died about 10 kilometres from this place as the crow flies and this is what we have been claiming all the time we know when he was killed too. And up until the 24th, well, everything that the Prosecution mentioned in the indictment, all those events had been finished, the mosque, et cetera. So these documents are of crucial importance because the unfortunate Cikota died at elevation 402 and it's only 10 kilometres from Sovici as the crow flies. It's up in the hills. And you can see who was assigned tasks and you can see who was engaged in Sovici. And Your Honour, this is why I suggest that at least the minutes of these three meetings, the 20th of April, the 21st of April, and the 6th of May, these three pages which are A4 format should be translated so that you can read them. We can forget about everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally, everything should be translated, but we could have at least these three documents rapidly translated, because when you say this is an exculpatory document, well, if this doesn't contradict the indictment, then I don't know what does. And if it doesn't contradict the testimony of witnesses. Your Honour, I have nothing else to say, unless there are any questions you would like to ask. But, Your Honour, I -- there was one thing I forgot: This is all stated in the indictment, which was in the court in Konjic. It's all in the court record, and I asked for this. The same facts are mentioned in the court record according to the indictment against these people who are mentioned here. And when we requested this from the Prosecution, we only received some of the records because again, we were told by the Prosecution that it wasn't important. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, we could probably be here for a very long time discussing the difference between testimony that might be relevant and testimony that is capable of being exculpatory. Much of what you read out, if not everything, is confirmatory of what we have heard from witnesses, but it doesn't advance your case because the prisoners were detained from the 20th of April allegedly until the 6th of May, and reading something to us on the 21st of April doesn't show that it's exculpatory, although it may have been relevant. But I have a few questions, with the leave of the President, to ask of the Prosecution for the moment. Mr. Scott, can you tell me on what basis the Prosecution decides a document is either relevant or exculpatory if it's not translated. I mean, how can you decide at an early stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document was reviewed -- first of all, some of the members of the investigation Prosecution team actually read a fair amount of Serbo-Croatian, number one. Secondly, it is commonplace in the OTP for documents to be reviewed with the assistance of a language assistants, to sit next to the language assistant, go through a document, have the document read out loud. In addition to that, there were indeed, as we said yesterday, some passages that were picked out and parts were translated, and those were also reviewed. So a number of ways, Your Honour, Judge Clark, and it's not unusual. It happens almost every day. The Prosecutor, a lawyer, an investigator, sits down with an untranslated document with an interpreter and goes through the document. That's how it was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Very good. And then the next point I want to make is do you have a response to make to Mr. Krsnik's valid assertion, his valid assertion that the contents of this fairly lengthy - it's not a diary, but collection of minutes - will indicate that there is nothing whatever to support the contention, the allegation by the Prosecution that the civilian prisoners, the women and children in the Junuzovici houses were guarded by the KB who played a role in their transfer?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge Clark. I'm trying to follow the full gist of the question. Your Honour, we -- it's again our position that the diary that -- excuse me, these minutes are fully consistent with the Prosecution case, as Your Honour noted just a moment ago. They were confirmatory. The fact that there were a number of people, clearly in the Sovici-Doljani area, there were different houses and different people being guarded in different places at different times. Now, Mr. Krsnik, he told us that he's been reading these documents every day since the 5th of March. The Chamber has been extremely patient with him this evening, took a break, gave him another 15 minutes. And despite that he's read the documents every day since the 5th of March and despite the fact that he had an additional 15 minutes he comes up with three passages and that's the best he can do, and none of those passages are inconsistent with the Prosecution case. Clearly the -- Mijat Tomic was involved in the area. Of course they were. They were the local battalion. That there were minutes of what they were doing and providing logistics and were helping civilians -- and I note it doesn't say prisoners in many instances it says civilians. There were Croat civilians that had to be cared for as well. Judge Clark, Your Honours, if those three instances are the best that he can do, it further confirms the Prosecution position that indeed nothing in this document is exculpatory. Just one other specific response: On the 6th of May, the Chamber will recall it was on the 4th of May that most of the women and children were in fact put on buses and expelled. There were some residual prisoners. It's on -- for instance, I have -- during the break I pulled out our final brief on Sovici-Doljani and on page 73 of our final brief it talks about on or about the 4th or 5th of May, approximately 470 Muslim women, children, and elderly were gathered from the Junuzovici houses and elsewhere and taken away. The fact that there were some residual civilians still in the area on the 6th of May, which may or may not have been guarded by the Mijat Tomic Battalion, is neither here nor there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think you're right about the 4th of May. I was surprised about that, and just assumed that I had made a mistake. Mr. Krsnik seems to be making the point that the documents by inference, because they fail to mention the Convicts Battalion or Mr. Tuta, exonerate him. But my recollection is that a document that you exhibited in your second motion actually was a document we saw in court mentions Mr. Tuta, but it is outside the period of the -- of the charge in the indictment. So it's not -- it's not correct to say that Mr. Tuta's name is never mentioned. But what he is saying, if I understand you correctly, Mr. Krsnik, is that rather like the indictment that's called the Konjic indictment, the absence of mention of the Convicts Battalion in material places and on material dates is capable of being exculpatory. Do I correctly paraphrase your argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I think that's correct, Your Honour, number one, and number two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I thought I had it on. I believe that would be correct. And it also, Your Honour, when we talk about exculpatory evidence, I seem to get a feeling from the Bench and from Your Honour Judge Clark that the exculpatory evidence somehow has to be pure exculpatory evidence. And I note that on page 37 you actually spoke about that. Exculpatory evidence could be pure exculpatory evidence. Because of the burden of proof in this proceeding and the burden of proof is on the Prosecution beyond a reasonable doubt, we have no burden of proof. We may bring up evidence that tends to cloud the evidence that the Prosecution presents, which then becomes exculpatory because it raises a reasonable doubt as to the evidence that's being presented by the Prosecution. So I get the feeling from some of the comments that the burden somehow is on the Defence to prove the innocence, and that's not the case. And we all know that, Your Honour, and I know that, you know that. But there are more forms of exculpatory evidence than the pure exculpatory evidence which I think you're looking for. Other types of exculpatory evidence could be evidence which goes to counter-evidence brought by the party that has the burden of proof, which would thereby raise a reasonable doubt, which would thereby stand for a not guilty finding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: We have to recall what the President said at the beginning of this case is that we were in the very final stages of our deliberation when we were asked to stay our deliberations, and therefore, he said, that the onus was on you at this stage, you the Defence, to prove to us that this particular series of documents that were recently disclosed were capable of being exculpatory and therefore to stop our deliberations. It's quite a different matter from something during a trial and it's quite technical. It's a very unusual situation that we all find ourselves in. But thank you anyway. I just think that Mr. Scott was attempting to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- during the break I pulled out the -- again, the Sovici-Doljani part of the closing brief, and obviously I read it quite quickly. But Your Honour, you know, the problem of course is we can sit here and argue and probably go all day tomorrow rearguing the whole case. Nothing that -- the three documents that Mr. Krsnik just took you to, the three items, which again I submit to you represents the high water mark of his efforts. That's the best he can do. And none of those documents when I reread the brief and what happened on which day and what prisoners were there, none of it is -- none of those things are inconsistent with the Prosecution's case. You know, again, without going through, simply pulling out transcripts of witnesses and rereading every Sovici-Doljani witness and showing you how nothing that's been said has been inconsistent, I just don't know how else to do it. We've reviewed it. Judge Clark, I assure you I meant what I said. When we reviewed the case -- when we found the document again in January and reviewed it, it was seriously considered. We went through it -- we went through the document. It was put against the evidence in the case. It was put against the charges, not all kinds of other things. We could talk about a gillion [phoen] places where Mr. Naletilic wasn't on a given day. He probably wasn't in Sarajevo in a given day either. He probably wasn't in Zagreb on a given day. That's beside the point. There's nothing in this document that is inconsistent with the Prosecution case or exculpates Mr. Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: What was the purpose, Mr. Scott? What was the purpose of serving them on the other side at this stage then? I mean, if they had -- they were so unimportant that you didn't need to serve them, why did you serve them? If they -- if they weren't exculpatory, why did you serve them? What could Mr. Krsnik reasonably have done with those papers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, probably nothing. In fact, he has done nothing with them. That's a separate issue. I've told the Chamber repeatedly in our papers and orally we did it out of an abundance of caution. Mr. Meek himself said to us an hour or so ago that the Rados diary was a hotly contested piece of evidence. When we reviewed the document again in January/February, and it was by Alojz Rados, concerning the same man in the same handwriting and it was a document that clearly does relate -- that doesn't makes it exculpatory but it does relate to another document that was hotly contested, and it was simply a judgment call. And as I said before, going the extra mile to say, "Look, we don't think it's exculpatory but let's simply give it to them." Now, they have the opportunity. They have had the opportunity in fact because we went the extra mile -- they've had the opportunity to come into this chamber, make written filings, and take two hours of this Chamber's time trying to argue and trying to convince you that it's exculpatory. They haven't done that. It's not the Prosecution's fault. The Prosecution went above and beyond what we thought we were required to do. The Chamber has given Mr. Krsnik every opportunity to make his case and he hasn't done so. That's our position. Mr. President, I must say that I had no -- I see Mr. Krsnik on his feet again. It's 7.00. I had no -- I have a personal obligation this evening. I had no idea that we were going to go on for hours on this. If you want to reschedule the hearing, Mr. President -- if you want the hearing to go on because Mr. Krsnik, as we know from past experience, will be on his feet as often as the Court will allow. Now, if we're going to continue, Mr. President, I ask the Chamber to recess and reschedule the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you know we are under a very tight schedule and we heard your case already. Would you please allow me to ask one question, just one question to the -- to Mr. Scott. Yes. The sitting will be over in five minutes, in five minutes. I just have one question to Mr. Scott. I'm very suspicious about that extra mile. I would like to know about on what legal basis did you disclose those materials? I understand on many occasions that if somebody Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. did something just out of abandoned caution and good faith, it's not good enough, that might be doing that in violation of the Rules of Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, let me say that I'm disappointed and saddened to hear that the Chamber would be suspicious. I thought the Prosecution has gone about its business in the last 18 months to try to indicate that we have been reliable and credible in our presentations to the Chamber, and I am deep -- I am saddened, saddened to hear that. I can only give the answer -- maybe it will help if I say it this way: I once had a Federal -- a respected Federal Judge in Denver, where I practiced before, in a case say, "Mr. Scott, you're a person not only who wears a belt but he also wears suspenders." And this is a case in which we simply said for all the reasons I've said -- Mr. President, I can only say what I've said before. We simply said, "Let's just give it to them." Let's avoid any issue about whether we disclosed it or not, length just simply give it over. Now, I've told Mr. -- I have to say I told Mr. Bos as a young lawyer, I said, "Mr. Bos, Roland, I suppose the moral of this story is don't do anything more than what you absolutely have to do." And if that is the moral of the story, that's very unfortunate. That's very unfortunate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, did you look into the Rule 66(C) and try to rely on that rule, or did you look into the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, especially on the Furundzija case where Judge Mumba, I believe, made a decision on similar situations?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I didn't look at any jurisprudence in the Tribunal. I looked at my heart and I said, "Let's disclose it." And it was disclosed. And now apparently we can only say -- perhaps we regret disclosing it because the Chamber's view seems to be if we were not strictly required to disclose it, then we should not have disclosed it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it's time to close this hearing, and this Trial Chamber will reserve its decision after deliberations on this very point. The hearing is adjourned.
